the recognition of taphonomic signatures that may be used as proxies to assess environmental conditions during reef development.
the recognition and characterization of taphonomic signatures of reefs that developed in nearshore, high-turbidity environments, where terrigenous-sediments are a major component of reef accretions.

the reef framework of Paluma Shoals, and presumably other nearshore, turbidity-zone reefs, is dominated by the deposition of coral clasts that are largely in situ, but are also reworked from the adjacent reef slope.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reefs of Paluma Shoals (and Lugger Shoal) are dominated by a high proportion of clast-supported framework.

the taphonomic signature of nearshore, inshore reefs is dominated by a suite of taphofacies that are characterized by: 1. the presence of isolated coral colonies and coral rubble, 2. a lack of cementation, and 3. the presence of abundant terrigenous sediment within intra-skeletal porosity.
the taphonomy of the reefs at Paluma and Lugger Shoals is similar to that of other nearshore, turbidity-impacted reefs in the central Great Barrier Reefs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the taphonomic signature of nearshore reefs is distinct from that of other reefs, and that the suite of taphofacies and associated taphonomic signatures that characterize these reefs are useful in the identification of such reefs.
the taphonomic signature of nearshore, high-turbidity reefs is distinct and can be readily recognized.
the taphonomic signature of turbid-zone reefs is distinct from that of reefs in other reef zones and that this signature can be used to identify such reefs in the geological record.
